rv.q: This lavishly mounted stage adaptation of the beloved 1964. Disney film proves that sometimes more really can be more, delivering a family-friendly spectacle that should enchant children and adults alike.
You may end up feeling a bit overstuffed, but, boy, the experience will be fun.
But reprise-laden excesses aside, there's much to savor here.
It's spectacular, and not even slightly boring, but anyone familiar with Walt Disney's 1964 film version of "Mary Poppins" is likely to come away asking what happened to the charm.

Well, she flies. She opens her parrot-handled umbrella, takes hold of her carpetbag, then soars out and up over the seats at the Theatre - presumably to a place where a magic nanny can hole up until required by the next unruly family. Excellent flying.
This almost Puritanical suspicion of theatrical enchantment for its own sake keeps 'Mary Poppins' from ever achieving the undiluted wonder.
Disney's Mary Poppins is a handsome, well-crafted family musical that delivers the goods without quite achieving greatness.

But anyone hoping that this show -- staged by director Richard Eyre and choreographer Matthew Bourne -- would provide much in the way of robust musical pleasure or emotional sustenance is likely to find it a wee bit of a letdown.
It is a roof-raising, toe-tapping, high-flying extravaganza.
This is a great show that, for first time this season, has Broadway singing again.

Forget the affable super-nanny of Disney's 1964 movie musical, Mary Poppins. As reconceived by director Richard Eyre (Iris) and codirector Matthew Bourne (the dance genius behind 1998's très gay Swan Lake), Mary (Ashley Brown) becomes a smug therapist to the cranky, morose Banks family.
Every element of the evening blends with an animated vivaciousness that lifts your spirits as easily as Mary Poppins takes off in flight, sailing to the upper balcony at the end of the evening.
Nevertheless, these are minor observations in a show that's brimming with hope, magic and humanity.
The biggest surprise of Mary Poppins—I can't believe I'm typing this—is that Disney has tried too hard to make a serious musical.
